body:
3.7.2 and 3.7.4 both deal with redirection. I would suggest grouping them together or putting them in a separate section.

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **3.7.1** | Verify that the application only uses client-side technologies which are still supported and considered secure. Examples of technologies which do not meet this requirement include NSAPI plugins, Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL, or client-side Java applets. | 2 | v5.0.be-50.8.2 |
| **3.7.2** | Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different hostname or domain (which is not controlled by the application) where the destination appears on an allowlist. | 2 | v5.0.be-50.8.5 |
| **3.7.3** | Verify that the application's top-level domain (e.g., site.tld) is added to the public preload list for HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). This ensures that the use of TLS for the application is built directly into the main browsers, rather than relying only on the Strict-Transport-Security response header field. | 3 | v5.0.be-50.8.4 |
| **3.7.4** | Verify that the application shows a notification when the user is being redirected to a URL outside of the application's control, with an option to cancel the navigation. | 3 | v5.0.be-50.8.1 |
| **3.7.5** | Verify that the application behaves as documented (such as warning the user or blocking access) if the browser used to access the application does not support the expected security features. | 3 | v5.0.be-50.8.3 |

comments.body:
For background, in ASVS v4.0.3 we had requirement that combined 3.7.2 and 3.7.4:
> v4.0.3-5.1.5 Verify that URL redirects and forwards only allow destinations which appear on an allow list, or show a warning when redirecting to potentially untrusted content.	

Via #1603 it was split, also note, that the level for them is different.

---

I think 3.7.2 should have "user" changed to "consumer" and to be moved to be together with 4.1.2.

Good idea. Perhaps something like:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **3.7.2** | Verify that automatic redirects only occur to allowlisted locations, and that only consumer-facing endpoints perform HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects, while service endpoints do not implement redirects to prevent data leakage. | 2 | v5.0.be-50.8.5 |

By "to be together," I meant that those 2 requirements should be in the same section; I did not want to propose merging them.

Also, @tghosth commented here https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1733#issuecomment-2826707445 that he is not into this move.

I get it now. 

I *think* Josh is ok with the redirect re-grouping, is ok with DOM clobbering move, but is not ok with prototype move. Is that right @tghosth ?

Either way, I think moving user to consumer for 3.7.4 and similar makes sense.

So, I don't want to merge them. They were deliberate split as 3.7.4 is more of a defense in depth L3 sort of requirement.

I still don't think we should move 3.7.2 either. It is not just relevant for API contexts and I still think it is more of a web browser thing anyway. I think in a non web browser setting, the user agent would need to take responsibility for understanding where it is being redirected and deciding whether it follows the redirect or not. Also, I am not sure what the attack scenario is for attacking a non browser user agent with an unvalidated redirect attack.

> It is not just relevant for API contexts

Proposed section is "V4.1 Generic Web Service Security" and is not limited to "API".

>  I still think it is more of a web browser thing anyway. 

Statistically, I agree. Technically, it is not limited to browser communication.

But we also have a requirement:
> V15.3.2 Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.

So I would say that the non-browser situation is covered by that and we can keep 3.7.2 where it is.

... or have somewhere dedicated "redirects" section.

> ... or have somewhere dedicated "redirects" section.

I realize that moving requirements around is painful right now. But redirect security is important and I dare say we want this as a separate section in say v15.

> So, I don't want to merge them.  They were deliberate split as 3.7.4 is more of a defense in depth L3 sort of requirement.

Agreed, I misread an early comment.

> I still don't think we should move 3.7.2 either.

I'm flexible in how, but I think its reasonable to group redirect requirements together.

> It is not just relevant for API contexts and I still think it is more of a web browser thing anyway. I think in a non web browser setting, the user agent would need to take responsibility for understanding where it is being redirected and deciding whether it follows the redirect or not. Also, I am not sure what the attack scenario is for attacking a non browser user agent with an unvalidated redirect attack.

There are quite a few non-browser scenarios when an API has an unvalidated redirect.

* Non-interactive agents follow redirects blindly. Most libraries treat a redirect as transport-level detail and reissue the request automatically, often carrying cookies or auth headers forward.
* Open redirects break the “internal-only” assumption. Once the first hop is inside the perimeter, any attacker-chosen Location: header becomes an data theft vector.  No user interaction is required. The attack is triggered by a background job, micro-service, or CI pipeline.

Carrying some bricks to build and brainstorm.

Redirecting consumer:
* V3.7.2 Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different hostname or domain (which is not controlled by the application) where the destination appears on an allowlist.
* V4.1.2 Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. This is to avoid a situation where a client is erroneously sending unencrypted HTTP requests, but since the requests are being automatically redirected to HTTPS, the leakage of sensitive data goes undiscovered.

Redirects and forwards being consumer or proxy:
* V15.3.2 Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.
* V4.2.2 Verify that any HTTP header field used by the application and defined by intermediary devices like load balancers or proxies, such as X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-*, cannot be overridden by the end-user.

V4.2.1 (maybe something else from V4.2.*) may match to this topic as well

Browser flow specific requirement, should stay in V3.7
* V3.7.4 Verify that the application shows a notification when the user is being redirected to a URL outside of the application's control, with an option to cancel the navigation.

Thanks for this summary Elar. My take on this is:

- 3.7.2 and 3.7.4 group well together, they would both be developed and tested together.

- 4.1.2  is more TLS configuration than redirect functionality and is usually minor TLS configuration or framework configuration
- 15.3.2 is more about SSRF protection and is usually a small library configuration flag in a HTTP client
- 4.2.2 looks more like trust boundary issues that redirect functionality

So the more I look at this, the only thing I would suggest is to put 3.7.2 and 3.7.4 next to each other instead of a small gap between them. Maybe even put those two is a different section in v3.
Then I prefer no action to take - to have them together it means 3.7.3 should be moved behind 3.7.4, but 3.7.3 is way more important requirement to be the 1st L3 requirement in this section.
I'm ok with that, but it does look a little strange to have a HSTS requirement in the middle of two redirect requirements in the same section.

@elarlang do you really think it is critical to have 3.7.3 before 3.7.4? It does feel like there is a small advantage in having two redirect related requirements next to each other, even if they are different levels.

> [@elarlang](https://github.com/elarlang) do you really think it is critical to have 3.7.3 before 3.7.4? It does feel like there is a small advantage in having two redirect related requirements next to each other, even if they are different levels.

Do I really think - no, it was not the wording I used. I said I prefer to keep things as they are. If there consensus that order of those 2 requirements solves some problem, then it can be changed.
So let's swap them, will you open the PR @elarlang so you can handle the mapping or should I?

Admittedly, this is low importance. It's just for organization and tidiness (better grouping of requirements) but it doesn't really solve anything.

If you want to wait until it's more convenient, like when we work on 5.01 or similar, I am ok with this.
